blocks.text: The servant in verses 1–7 speaks as one called and formed for a task, yet verse 3 names the servant “Israel,” while verses 5–6 describe the servant’s work as bringing Jacob and Israel back. Isaiah uses several voices and forms of address, so the speaker should be identified from the passage itself rather than assumed in advance. The singular servant language has been read in different ways—as individual, collective, prophetic, royal, or messianic—and the chapter does not by itself settle every later interpretive question. It is also important to distinguish what the passage says in its own setting from later quotations, allusions, and religious readings of it.

Isaiah 49 belongs to a larger book preserved in several ancient manuscript witnesses. The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete copy of all sixty-six chapters. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition, while also containing many spelling and some substantive differences; other Qumran manuscripts and interpretive writings show that Isaiah was actively copied and interpreted.
